newsitem.title: USA: Senators seek FTC probe of computer data bases.
newsitem.headline: Senators seek FTC probe of computer data bases.

text.p: Responding to a recent uproar over online data base company Lexis-Nexis, three senators have asked regulators to probe whether companies that run computer data bases violate consumers' right to privacy.

The Oct. 8 letter to Federal Trade Commission Chairman Robert Pitofsky also seeks advice on any new laws needed to protect consumers' privacy in the emerging electronic age, where reams of data about individuals can be had via computer.

"We have received calls and letters from constituents who are greatly disturbed about the compilation, sale, and usage of these data-bases," wrote Sens. Richard Bryan (D-Nev.), Larry Pressler (R-S.D.), and Ernest Hollings (D-S.C.).

"They, as well as consumers in general, are concerned about the potential intrustion upon, and violation of, individual privacy rights. There also is concern about the potential abusive and unlawful usage of the data."

Pressler chairs the commerce committee and Hollings is the senior Democrat. Bryan is the senior Democrat on the banking committee. The letter comes after Lexis-Nexis was bombarded by complaints last month from consumers over its "P-TRAK" computer file.
The file markets personal information to lawyers and others in the legal community trying to locate parties to a lawsuit, heirs and others involved in a case.

In a sign of consumer outrage, an electronic message zapped over the Internet computer network charged that P-TRAK was peddling Social Security numbers and mothers' maiden names, raising fears that such information could be used to generate credit-card scams.

Lexis, a unit of Reed-Elsevier PLC, said it ended access to Social Security data earlier this year after complaints. P-TRAK does offer a variety of other personal information, such as names, addersses, phone numbers.

Meanwhile, recent news accounts have reported that savvy computer users can go elsewhere online to unearth information such as Social Security numbers, driver's license reigstrations and other information.

The senators called on the FTC to investigate the compilation, sale and use of electronically transmitted data bases that include "identifiable personal information of private citizens without their knowledge."

In particular, they asked the FTC to look into whether compiling and selling such information without consumer consent violates the law, and whether the data bases create the potential for fraud and abuse.
The FTC was asked to provide a report within six months and to include recommedations for any new laws. The agency already has recommended more privacy protections.
